rewritten_text:
After a while you’d wake up and look around to see what had disturbed you. Maybe a steamboat was coughing its way upstream, so far across the river that you could only tell whether its paddle wheel was at the back or on the sides. Then for an hour or so there would be nothing to hear or see—just complete loneliness. Next a raft might drift past far away, with some fellow chopping wood, as people on rafts nearly always seem to do. You’d see his axe flash and fall without hearing a sound. It would rise again, and only when it was above his head would the thunk reach you. The sound had taken that long to cross the water. That was how we spent our days, lazing around and listening to the silence. Once a heavy fog came down, and passing rafts and boats banged tin pans to keep steamboats from running into them. A flatboat or raft passed so close that we could clearly hear the people talking, swearing, and laughing, but we couldn’t see them at all. It gave you the shivers, like spirits carrying on in the air. Jim thought they really were spirits, but I said:

“No. Spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Damn this damned fog.’”

As soon as it was dark, we pushed off. Once we reached about the middle of the river, we left the raft alone and let the current carry it wherever it pleased. Then we lit our pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about everything. We went naked day and night whenever the mosquitoes allowed it. The new clothes Buck’s family had made for me were too fine to feel comfortable, and I never cared much for clothes anyway.

Sometimes we had the whole river to ourselves for ages. Across the water lay the banks and islands, with perhaps a tiny light from a candle in a cabin window. Sometimes another light or two shone on the water, from a raft or flatboat, and maybe the sound of a fiddle or a song came drifting over. Living on a raft is lovely. Above us the sky was scattered with stars. We used to lie on our backs, stare at them, and discuss whether somebody had made them or they had simply happened. Jim thought they had been made, but I thought they had happened. Making so many, I figured, would have taken too long.

“Get up! What are you doing?”

I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to work out where I was. The sun was already up, and I’d been fast asleep. Pap stood over me, looking sour and sick. He said:

“What are you doing with that gun?”

I figured he didn’t remember anything he’d done, so I said:

“Someone tried to get in, and I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“I tried, but I couldn’t. I couldn’t get you to move.”

“Well, all right. Don’t stand there talking all day. Get outside and see if there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll be along in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I hurried up the riverbank. I noticed bits of branches and other things floating downstream, with a scattering of bark, so I knew the river had started rising. I reckoned I’d be having a wonderful time if I were back in town. The June rise always brought me luck: as soon as it began, firewood came floating down, along with pieces of timber rafts, sometimes a dozen logs still together. All you had to do was catch them and sell them to the woodyards or the sawmill.

I walked up the bank, keeping one eye out for Pap and the other on whatever the rising water might bring. Suddenly a canoe came along—a real beauty, about thirteen or fourteen feet long, floating high like a duck. I shot headfirst off the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and swam toward it. I expected someone to be lying inside, because people often played that trick. Once a fellow had rowed his little boat almost alongside, they would sit up and laugh at him. But this time there was nobody. It really was an empty drifting canoe, and I climbed in and paddled ashore. The old man would be pleased to see this, I thought; it was worth ten dollars. Yet when I reached shore, Pap still wasn’t in sight. As I guided it into a narrow creek, almost a gully, overhung with vines and willows, another idea struck me. I could hide it carefully, then, instead of escaping through the woods, travel fifty miles or so downriver and settle in one place. That would spare me the hardship of trudging along on foot.

I was quite near the shack, and all the time I imagined I heard the old man coming. But I managed to hide the canoe. Then I climbed out and peered around a clump of willows. There was the old man a little way down the path, aiming his gun at a bird.

Presently we heard his voice raised in a kind of halloo.

“How much farther I got to go?”

“How high have you climbed?” Legrand asked.

“Ever so far,” answered the negro; “I can see de sky through de tree-top.”

“Never mind the sky; listen to my instructions. Look down the trunk and count the branches beneath you on this side. How many have you gone past?”

“One, two, three, four, five—I passed five great limbs, massa, on dis side.”

“Climb one branch higher, then.”

A few minutes later his voice came again, reporting that he had reached the seventh limb.

“Now, Jup,” Legrand cried, plainly in great excitement, “I want you to make your way along that branch as far as possible. Tell me if you notice anything unusual.” Whatever small doubt I had retained about my unfortunate friend’s madness now vanished altogether. I could only conclude that lunacy had overtaken him, and I grew gravely concerned about bringing him home. As I considered the best course to pursue, Jupiter called out once more.

“I’m mighty afraid to go far out on dis branch—it’s dead pretty near all de way.”

“Did you say the limb was dead, Jupiter?” Legrand exclaimed, his voice trembling.

“Yes, massa, dead as a door-nail—finished for certain—done left dis life.”

“What in Heaven’s name am I to do?” Legrand asked, apparently in the utmost distress.

“Do?” I said, pleased at the chance to put in a word. “Why, return home and get to bed. Come along, there’s a good fellow! It grows late, and you must remember your promise.”

“Jupiter,” he shouted, paying me no attention whatever, “can you hear me?”

“Yes, Massa Will, hear you clear enough.”

“Then test the wood carefully with your knife and judge whether it is very rotten.”

“It’s rotten all right, massa,” the negro answered after a few moments, “but not as rotten as it might be. I could risk a little way out on de branch by myself, that’s true.”

“By yourself! What are you talking about?”

“I mean de bug. It’s a mighty heavy bug. If I drop him first, de branch won’t break with only one negro’s weight.”

“You infernal rascal!” cried Legrand, visibly relieved. “What do you mean by giving me such nonsense? Drop that beetle and I shall certainly break your neck. Attend to me, Jupiter—do you hear?”

“Yes, massa; no need to shout at a poor negro so.”

“Well, listen now. Venture along the limb as far as you consider safe, keep hold of the beetle, and I shall give you a silver dollar the moment you come down.”
